nodes.pain_point: I'm working all the time and still behind
inner_thoughts: I teach 6 days a week. I mark papers on Sunday. I don't remember the last time I had a full day off.
I'm working more hours than I ever have, but I feel like I'm getting less done.
I became a teacher because I love helping students. I spend maybe 60% of my time actually doing that.
nodes.intro_body: Working constantly and still feeling behind is a signal — not that you need to work harder, but that too much of your time is going to the wrong things.

strategies.title: Name your one full day off — and make it non-negotiable
content_paragraphs: Teaching six days a week and spending Sunday on admin is not dedication. It is a system that is broken. The teachers who sustain 10+ year careers without burning out almost all share one habit: they protect at least one full day where they do not teach, do not reply, and do not plan.
Write this down: "[Day] is my full day off. No teaching, no WhatsApp, no prep." Then tell a family member or colleague — accountability makes it stick.
This single commitment changes how you structure every other day in the week. When you know Sunday is protected, you stop letting Saturday bleed into it.

strategies.title: Time-block your week before anyone else fills it
content_paragraphs: Most teachers have teaching hours and then everything else bleeding into the gaps. Time-blocking means deciding in advance: these hours are teaching, these are prep, these are off. If it is not in the calendar, it gets filled by whatever arrives first.
Every Sunday evening, block teaching prep, marking, and your full day off before the week starts. Two 90-minute prep windows minimum.
What gets scheduled gets done. What does not get scheduled gets interrupted.

strategies.title: Set your response windows — and publish them
content_paragraphs: Every WhatsApp notification during a teaching session is a boundary failure, not a communication priority. You do not have to reply immediately. You feel like you do because you never told parents when you do reply.
Set two 45-minute response windows. Send the announcement to all parents this week: "I respond to messages between 6-7pm and 9-10pm on weekdays. For urgent matters, call me directly."
Parents adjust to this faster than you expect. The adjustment starts with you, not them.

strategies.title: Say no to scope creep — protect what you were hired to teach
content_paragraphs: Parents ask for extras: catch-up lessons, out-of-scope subject help, marking for classes you do not teach, emergency sessions the night before a paper. Every unplanned yes adds unpaid hours and chips away at your boundaries.
Write down what your fee covers. Anything outside that scope is a separate conversation with a separate fee — or a polite no.
Scope creep does not make you more valuable. It makes you more available, which is not the same thing.

strategies.title: Track your total weekly hours once — the number changes everything
content_paragraphs: You do not need to change anything yet. Just count one week: teaching, prep, admin, parent messages, marking, travel, and quick replies. Add them up.

Most teachers who feel like they are always working are clocking 55-70 hours per week. Seeing that number written down is usually the thing that makes every other strategy in this list feel non-negotiable.
Do this audit once. It takes one week. The result stays with you.

next.label: Test papers and marking take forever

nodes.pain_point: Test papers and marking take forever
inner_thoughts: I spent 4 hours on Saturday marking 30 papers. By the end I wasn't giving real feedback — I was just trying to finish.
I create a new test paper from scratch every month. I don't know why I don't just reuse them.
My students ask me for more practice papers. I want to give them more. But creating them takes as long as marking them.
nodes.intro_body: Marking and paper creation are the two most time-consuming teaching tasks — and both can be dramatically reduced with the right format changes.

strategies.title: MCQ practice tests: self-correcting in 5 minutes
content_paragraphs: A 20-question MCQ practice test can be peer-corrected in class by exchanging papers and reading answers aloud. No collection, no marking pile to take home. 5 minutes in class.
Design your regular practice tests in MCQ format where the subject allows. O/L and A/L exam papers include MCQ sections — your practice aligns to real exam format.
You're not compromising quality. You're removing marking time while making practice more exam-relevant.

strategies.title: Build a question bank — stop writing from scratch
content_paragraphs: After each test, save the questions you wrote to a master document organized by topic and difficulty. After 6 months, you have 80–100 questions per topic.
Future tests are assembled in 10 minutes by picking questions from the bank. The first year is investment. Every year after is return.
You've already written the questions. They exist in old test papers. Spend one afternoon organizing them — you'll never start from scratch again.

strategies.title: Compile a comprehensive past paper pack — once
content_paragraphs: 5–10 years of past papers, organized by topic and year, printed and bound (or distributed as PDF). Distribute at the start of the year.
The most useful practice material already exists. You don't need to create it — you need to curate it.
A student working through a 5-year past paper pack practices every question type that will appear in the exam. That's better than anything you'd write, and it takes you one afternoon to compile.

strategies.title: Marking rubrics cut structured question time in half
content_paragraphs: For structured and essay-style questions, a marking rubric defines what gets marks, how many, and for exactly what content.

Create rubrics for your 10 most common question types once. With a rubric, marking a structured question takes 60 seconds — check, tick, add up. Without one, it takes 3–5 minutes as you re-read and re-decide every time.
A marking rubric is your own decision made once and applied many times.

visual.text: A rubric for 30 structured papers saves 1–2 hours of marking per test session. Across a year of monthly tests, that's 12–24 hours returned to you.

strategies.title: At 150+ students, consider a marking assistant
content_paragraphs: A final-year undergraduate or a student who recently scored well in the subject can mark MCQ and structured responses against your rubric. Pay per paper or a fixed monthly amount.
At 150 students × 4 practice tests per month = 600 papers. At your time value, that's 40–60 hours of marking. A marking assistant does it for LKR 30,000–60,000 — less than 20% of one month's revenue.
Your expertise is the teaching. The marking against a rubric is a mechanical task.

next.label: I can't keep up with parent messages

nodes.pain_point: I can't keep up with parent messages
inner_thoughts: I got a WhatsApp message at 11:23pm asking if fees were due next week. I lay there wondering if I should reply.
I answered 'what time is class on Saturday?' four times yesterday. Four different parents. Same day.
There are 47 unread messages from parents in my WhatsApp right now. I know some are important but I can't face opening it.
nodes.intro_body: The volume of parent messages isn't a people problem — it's a systems problem. The messages exist because information gaps exist. Close the gaps and the messages stop.

strategies.title: Switch to broadcast lists — immediately
content_paragraphs: A WhatsApp broadcast sends the same message to many parents but lands in each person's private chat. No group thread, no parent-to-parent conversations to moderate.
One broadcast per batch. One update per week. Schedule changes, fee reminders, exam announcements — one message reaches everyone.
The parents who reply individually will still reply. But you've eliminated the need to send 30 individual messages and manage 30 simultaneous threads.

strategies.title: Set response windows — tell parents at enrollment
content_paragraphs: "I respond to WhatsApp between 9–10am and 7–8pm." Written in your enrollment materials. Stated clearly on day one.
This isn't rude — it's professional. A doctor doesn't take calls during surgery. You don't take messages during class. When parents know this from day one, they don't feel ignored.
Parents who message at 11pm will stop expecting a reply. Parents who message at 9:05am will get one within the hour.

strategies.title: Build template replies for your top 5 questions
content_paragraphs: The same 5 questions arrive every week. "What time is class?" "How do I pay?" "Is there class on Poya?" "How is my child doing?" "What's the fee for this month?"
Save template answers as saved messages in WhatsApp. When the message arrives: 2 taps, done.
This doesn't feel significant until you realize you've been typing the same 30-word message 8 times a week for 3 years.

visual.label: Example saved reply — fee question
visual.text: Hi! Fees for this month are LKR [amount], due by the 1st. You can pay cash at class or scan the QR code on the whiteboard. Thank you!

strategies.title: Give every new parent a FAQ at enrollment
content_paragraphs: Class schedule, fee amount, due date, payment method, your response window, what happens if their child misses class — one page, given at enrollment.
For current parents who've never had this, send it now. "Here's a quick reference for everything you might want to know — hope it's useful!"
These answers stop at least 60% of the messages before they ever start.

strategies.title: Proactive updates stop reactive questions
content_paragraphs: A parent who received a monthly progress update last week won't message asking "how is my child doing?" A parent who got a fee reminder on the 25th won't message on the 2nd asking if they owe anything.
Most parent messages are filling information vacuums you left. The single most effective thing you can do is send one proactive update per month per student.
One message sent by you prevents 5–8 incoming messages.
